description: We are a motivated bunch of engineers who are eager to explore and know the unkown
summary: SPHEREx Voyage is a website that lets anyone — students, local scientists, or curious observers — pick a patch of sky and see how SPHEREx actually imaged it over time. Using real SPHEREx images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), each image is linked to its original observation date and wavelength, and every pixel the archive flags as unreliable is highlighted. This addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, which asks for a tool showing how SPHEREx observes a selected field at different times. The key idea is honesty about uncertainty: two images of the same patch can differ for reasons unrelated to the sky — clipped cutouts, saturated detector pixels, or differing wavelengths — so false discoveries are easy to make. Rather than asking users whether images look different, Voyage runs a single, standardized quality check at the requested position and shows why a difference might not be real. Tested on five challenge targets and 20 verified archive files, it accepts 7 of 15 dated cutouts and rejects the rest, turning raw survey data into a trustworthy, date-true visual comparison.
details:
What it does and how it works. SPHEREx Voyage is a web tool for exploring how NASA's SPHEREx telescope imaged a chosen patch of sky across different observing dates and wavelengths. The user either selects one of five preset targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) or enters a right ascension and declination. The tool pulls real SPHEREx exposures from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), each carrying its own observation date, wavelength, source link, and checksum. A quality screen checks the data-quality flags at the requested pixel before anything is compared: a pixel is accepted only if no flags beyond SOURCE and FULLSAMPLE are set, and otherwise it is shown as rejected rather than hidden. Results are explored in two deliberately separate views: a Time view (one image per observing date on a shared sky grid and brightness scale) and a Wavelength view (102 channels of a combined mosaic, which has no single observing date).

Benefits and impact. Two images of the same sky can differ for reasons unrelated to the sky itself: cutouts clipped at a detector edge, saturated or bloomed pixels, or a slightly different wavelength, which makes false discoveries easy. Rather than asking "are these different?", Voyage shows why a difference may not be real. Across the five challenge fields, our single quality check accepts 7 of 15 dated cutouts and rejects 8; for RW Aurigae and R Draconis the requested center pixel is unusable on every date. Without these flags, RW Aurigae's center would appear to brighten by roughly 90% between observations, a convincing but invalid "measurement." The tool helps students see how a real survey image looks and where it has gaps, lets local scientists sanity-check a candidate finding against the archive's own flags before reporting it, and gives teachers ready examples of variability and motion.

Tools and data. Built on real SPHEREx data (Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3) accessed through IRSA, including the IRSA Mosaic Tool for the 102-channel cubes. FITS images were read and their header and flag extensions decoded in Python; proper-motion and position calculations use Astropy, and aperture-photometry background relations follow Photutils. Published proper motions, spectra, and variability periods are taken from the cited literature.

Creativity and factors considered. The design is driven by numbers rather than guesswork. We verified that half-year proper-motion shifts for these targets are only about 1 to 2 pixels (6.15 arcseconds per pixel), so the prototype never depicts a moved object. We showed that RW Aurigae's brightness changes depend on wavelength, so every dated image lists its wavelength and the difference view warns when wavelengths differ. We confirmed that three visits over about 1.4 periods cannot establish R Draconis's roughly 246-day pulsation period, so no period is fitted. Throughout, the tool is honest about its limits: it does not identify the objects, measure brightness or motion, or declare any discovery. It performs visual inspection and quality checking, the first step toward real measurement.
